title: The Rise of Agentic AI: Transforming Legal and Enterprise Workflows
author: Jerry Levine

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core copilot and work-redesign proposition, while materially extending it with a concrete architecture: domain-specific models, dynamically routed agents, parallel execution and human review orchestrated across end-to-end workflows. Its stronger autonomy and performance claims are largely promotional and weakly evaluated, but it still recognizes human oversight, use-case specialization, ROI and risk controls as deployment constraints.
qs: The latest transformation in AI involves specialized AI agents working together in an orchestrated manner, ensuring seamless collaboration between models and human experts.
This partnership approach ensures that AI enhances rather than replaces human expertise.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Levine accepts the cluster’s core account of agentic AI as coordinated, multi-step delegation across specialised tools, with routine autonomy bounded by human judgment and escalation. He also acknowledges risk controls and uncertain ROI, although he gives little attention to error propagation or verification as the resulting bottleneck and relies mainly on product claims and forecasts rather than comparative evidence.
qs: The latest transformation in AI involves specialized AI agents working together in an orchestrated manner, ensuring seamless collaboration between models and human experts.
Agentic AI augments human decision-making by providing draft clauses, contract summaries, and compliance recommendations while allowing legal professionals to refine outputs.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Levine supports the cluster’s operating-model framing by presenting agentic AI as workflow-level automation integrated with enterprise systems and bounded by human oversight. His Gartner-based warning about project cancellations also aligns with the cluster’s caution that returns depend on clear value and risk controls, although he does not substantively address provider bargaining, ALSPs or pricing change.
qs: Deeper enterprise integration for AI-driven contract management, compliance, and advisory services will become standard practice as organizations recognize the competitive advantages these systems provide.

However, over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls, according to Gartner predictions, highlighting the importance of choosing proven solutions with clear ROI.

kp.k: Agentic systems orchestrate specialized, semi-autonomous legal workflows
kp.d: The document describes a transition from isolated, repetitive AI tasks to coordinated agents that make decisions and adapt within predefined conditions. It presents multi-LLM architectures and task-specific models as foundations for automating complex, multi-step legal processes, asserting greater accuracy and adaptability without presenting comparative testing.
qs: AI agents are semi-autonomous systems that can make decisions, dynamically control their own processes, and take actions to achieve specific goals with limited human interaction.
These agents operate within predefined conditions while maintaining the flexibility to adapt their approach based on context and requirements.
This orchestration enables complex, multi-step processes to be automated while maintaining quality and compliance.

kp.k: Enterprise adoption figures mix reported deployment and forecasts
kp.d: The document attributes to Gartner a forecast that 40% of enterprise applications will integrate task-specific agents by 2026, compared with less than 5% today. Separately, it reports a Gartner poll in which 24% of CIOs and IT function leaders had deployed fewer than a dozen agents and another 4% had deployed over a dozen as of May 2025. These are enterprise-wide figures, not measures of legal-sector adoption; no poll sample size is supplied.
qs: With 40% of enterprise applications expected to integrate task-specific AI agents by 2026, up from less than 5% today, according to Gartner, organizations are rapidly adopting these intelligent systems to transform contract management, compliance, and operational efficiency.

According to a Gartner poll, 24% of CIOs and IT function leaders had already deployed a few AI agents (less than a dozen) and another 4% had deployed over a dozen as of May 2025, according to Gartner research.

kp.k: Contract automation spans review, redlining, negotiation and compliance
kp.d: The author claims that agents can combine contract analysis, jurisdiction-specific redlining, internal-policy checks and risk mitigation in a single workflow. Unnamed examples illustrate applications across vendor agreements, leases, clinical trials and supply-chain contracts; they are presented without supporting case-study methods or measured outcomes. Cross-functional integration is also proposed for procurement, HR and compliance.
qs: A multinational corporation uses Leah to analyze vendor contracts for legal risks, suggest redlines based on jurisdiction-specific regulations, and ensure compliance with internal policies—all within one automated workflow.
A multinational corporation integrates Leah across procurement, HR, and compliance teams, ensuring standardized workflows and improving cross-department collaboration.

kp.k: Human oversight coexists with autonomous routine-task execution
kp.d: The document frames AI as augmenting rather than replacing legal expertise: agents prepare clauses, summaries and compliance recommendations, while lawyers refine outputs and maintain strategic alignment. At the same time, it claims routine end-to-end work can proceed without human intervention. Its insurance example specifically assigns in-house counsel the review and refinement of generated policy amendments, and it asserts that human corrections improve subsequent suggestions.
qs: The ability to handle end-to-end processes without human intervention for routine tasks is transforming how legal departments operate.
Agentic AI augments human decision-making by providing draft clauses, contract summaries, and compliance recommendations while allowing legal professionals to refine outputs.
An insurance company's legal team uses Leah to generate policy amendments while in-house counsel reviews and refines AI-suggested changes.
The system learns from human corrections and preferences, continuously improving its suggestions over time.

kp.k: Automation promises staffing scalability and reduced external-counsel reliance
kp.d: The author argues that legal departments can increase throughput without proportional staffing growth and that automated contract work reduces reliance on external counsel. An unnamed financial-institution example describes shifting legal teams from repetitive reviews toward high-value negotiations. These are asserted organizational effects and illustrative applications, rather than quantified employment or outside-spend findings.
qs: Organizations are finding that AI-powered workflows can handle increasing volumes of work without proportional increases in staffing.
Organizations leverage Leah to automate contract review, redlining, and negotiation, reducing reliance on external counsel and accelerating deal closure.
A financial institution automates due diligence processes with Leah, freeing legal teams to focus on high-value negotiations rather than repetitive contract reviews.

kp.k: Time-saving claims accompany broader economic automation projections
kp.d: The document reports contract review falling from days to hours and processing-time reductions of up to 90%, without identifying organizations, samples or measurement methods. It separately cites McKinsey's projection that activities accounting for up to 30 percent of current US working hours could be automated by 2030. That projection concerns the whole economy, not legal work specifically.
qs: Organizations report reducing contract review times from days to hours, with some processes seeing up to 90% reduction in processing time.
By 2030, activities that account for up to 30 percent of hours currently worked across the US economy could be automated—a trend accelerated by generative AI, according to McKinsey research.

kp.k: Compliance accuracy rests on claimed specialization and model routing
kp.d: The author attributes improved legal accuracy to domain-specific models, parallel agents and dynamic selection of models suited to particular tasks. It claims that legally trained agents minimize errors and identify regulatory risks, including potential HIPAA violations in an unnamed healthcare example. The document supplies no accuracy benchmark or error-rate evidence for its assurance that no critical issues are overlooked.
qs: Leah dynamically selects the best AI models for each task, optimizing performance and accuracy.
AI agents trained on legal and regulatory frameworks minimize errors and proactively identify compliance risks.
The consistency of AI-driven compliance checks ensures that no critical issues are overlooked, even in high-volume scenarios.

kp.k: Customer-service forecasts illustrate wider autonomous-work expectations
kp.d: As cross-domain context for end-to-end automation, the document cites Gartner's prediction that agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer-service issues by 2029 and reduce operational costs by 30%. This is a customer-service forecast, not evidence of equivalent legal-service performance or savings.
qs: By 2029, agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention, leading to a 30% reduction in operational costs, according to Gartner predictions.

kp.k: Costs, uncertain value and risk controls threaten deployments
kp.d: The document qualifies its adoption narrative with Gartner's prediction that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. It uses that prediction to recommend selecting proven solutions with clear return on investment; this is not a reported cancellation rate.
qs: However, over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls, according to Gartner predictions, highlighting the importance of choosing proven solutions with clear ROI.

kp.k: Future negotiation agents retain escalation boundaries
kp.d: The author describes real-time contract-negotiation agents as emerging and predicts that they will operate within predetermined parameters while escalating complex issues to humans. It also anticipates improved enterprise-specific learning and deeper integration into contract management, compliance and advisory services. Separately, Gartner is quoted forecasting autonomous execution of at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions by 2028, up from zero percent in 2024; this is not a legal-sector-specific forecast.
qs: AI agents capable of real-time contract negotiation are emerging, allowing for faster deal closure and more efficient business operations.
These systems will negotiate within predetermined parameters while escalating complex issues to human professionals.
AI models that continuously learn from enterprise-specific data will become more sophisticated, improving their accuracy and relevance over time.
by 2028, at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agentic AI, up from zero percent in 2024

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jerry Levine presents agentic AI as a means of automating multi-step legal workflows, augmenting lawyers, expanding capacity without proportional hiring, and reducing costs and reliance on external counsel.
pts.d: Levine claims that collaborating, task-specific agents can combine contract analysis, jurisdiction-specific redlining, risk mitigation and policy compliance in end-to-end workflows, performing routine tasks without human intervention. He also describes an augmentation model in which agents produce clauses, summaries and recommendations that lawyers review and refine, with systems improving through human feedback. He claims that legal departments can process greater volumes without proportional staffing increases, that contract reviews fall from days to hours, and that some processes achieve up to 90% shorter processing times. He says automation frees lawyers for high-value negotiations, reduces reliance on external counsel and accelerates deal closure. Further claims include more accurate outputs from specialized models than general-purpose AI; identification of risks human reviewers might miss; consistent cross-jurisdictional compliance; parallel processing and task-dependent model selection; and standardized workflows across procurement, HR and compliance. His future-facing claims include deeper integration becoming standard, emerging real-time negotiation within predetermined parameters with escalation to humans, and increasingly enterprise-specific learning. The article also incorporates wider enterprise adoption, autonomous decision-making, customer-service automation and economy-wide hours-automation forecasts, rather than treating these as legal-sector measurements.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Levine supports the account with attributed Gartner and McKinsey research, product-capability descriptions and illustrative enterprise examples; the legal-workflow benefits are not accompanied by named-client measurements or benchmark methods.
pts.d: The article is a vendor-associated account promoting Leah. Levine cites Gartner for an enterprise-application adoption forecast, a May 2025 CIO/IT-leader deployment poll, customer-service automation and cost forecasts, autonomous-work-decision projections, and predicted project cancellations. He cites McKinsey for possible automation of activities accounting for up to 30% of US working hours by 2030. These provide cross-enterprise context, not direct measurements of Leah's legal performance. The legal examples involve unnamed multinational, Fortune 500, financial, healthcare, technology, logistics, pharmaceutical, real-estate and insurance organizations and an unnamed law firm. They are presented as examples without enough information to establish whether they are documented deployments or illustrative scenarios. The days-to-hours and up-to-90% processing-time claims are attributed only to unspecified organizational reports, without sample sizes, baselines or measurement methods. Claims about accuracy, comprehensive compliance, feedback-driven improvement and reduced external-counsel use are supported by descriptions and examples rather than comparative test results. No legal benchmark or quantified legal error-rate study is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 article presents most legal capabilities as available now, while cited forecasts run from 2026 to 2030; autonomy is bounded by task conditions, human oversight and implementation risks.
pts.d: Levine describes current legal automation and savings in the present tense, without specifying deployment durations or when the reported improvements were measured. The Gartner adoption forecast is 40% of enterprise applications by 2026, versus less than 5% 'today'; the deployment poll is dated May 2025. He reports Gartner's prediction that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 because of costs, unclear value or inadequate risk controls; at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be autonomous by 2028, versus zero in 2024; and 80% of common customer-service issues will be autonomously resolved by 2029, with a 30% reduction in operational costs. The cited McKinsey projection concerns activities representing up to 30% of US working hours by 2030, not a stated percentage of jobs eliminated. No specific deadline is attached to deeper legal integration becoming standard or more sophisticated enterprise learning. Levine qualifies autonomy through predefined conditions, routine-task boundaries, human review and escalation of complex negotiation issues. He emphasizes clear ROI and adequate risk controls as implementation considerations. His claimed up-to-90% processing improvement applies to 'some processes,' not all legal work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal beneficiaries identified are enterprise legal departments and their business counterparts; lawyers retain review and strategic work, while external counsel may face reduced client reliance.
pts.d: Levine focuses on corporate buyers of legal services, particularly large, multinational and regulated enterprises. In-house lawyers are described as reviewing AI-generated changes and moving away from repetitive review toward negotiations and strategic judgment. Legal departments gain capacity without proportional staffing growth; the article does not specify layoffs, associate staffing structures or changes to lawyer promotion. External counsel is affected through an asserted reduction in corporate dependence, but no quantified market-share or revenue effect is given. Procurement, HR and compliance teams are described as benefiting from common processes and cross-department coordination. Sector-specific examples address healthcare privacy compliance, pharmaceutical clinical-trial contracts, financial regulatory reporting, insurance amendments, logistics supply-chain risk and real-estate leases. An unnamed law-firm example concerns case-law and precedent analysis using different models. Broader forecasts concern enterprise applications, CIOs and IT leaders, customer-service operations and US work activities. Leah is presented as a software solution, not as a provider delivering legal work outside the traditional law-firm form. The article does not make a concrete access-to-justice claim for individuals or small organizations.
